Each [Continuum of Care](#term:continuum-of-care) designates an HMIS lead; SSVF grantees must enter data and export it monthly; [Grant](#term:grant) and Per Diem grantees are encouraged to use it [1286](#cite:1286) [1309](#cite:1309) [1312](#cite:1312).

name: CDFI Fund Awards Management Information System (AMIS)
what: The [CDFI](#term:cdfi) Fund's own application system: an applicant creates an AMIS account, submits the [SF-424](#term:sf-424) through [Grants.gov](#term:grants-gov) and then submits the application in AMIS [1434](#cite:1434).

name: EDA EDGE portal (sfgrants.eda.gov)
what: EDA's application portal for its rolling notices [1431](#cite:1431) [1430](#cite:1430).

name: LITC grants portal (litcgrants.treasury.gov)
what: The site where Low Income Taxpayer Clinic applications are submitted, as stated in the 2027 [Grants.gov](#term:grants-gov) listing [1439](#cite:1439).

name: Idaho National Laboratory proposals portal
what: Applications to the DOE Office of Nuclear Energy infrastructure notice are submitted at proposals.inl.gov [1588](#cite:1588).

name: EPSCoR jurisdiction prerequisites (steering committee and Science and Technology Plan)
what: Before any organisation in a jurisdiction may submit to E-CORE or E-RISE, the jurisdiction must have an active Jurisdictional Steering Committee and a Science and Technology Plan approved within the past five years [1520](#cite:1520) [1522](#cite:1522).

name: Grant Eligibility Application (GEA) system at HEPIS.ed.gov
what: The Department of Education system in which an institution checks its [Title III](#term:title-iii-v-eligibility) eligibility designation and files a reconsideration or waiver request; it is reached with a [Login.gov](#term:login-gov) account [1596](#cite:1596).

name: HUD Disaster Recovery Grant Reporting system (DRGR)
what: The HUD system in which an earmarked Economic Development Initiative grantee returns its [grant](#term:grant) package, enters an Action Plan, files semi-annual reports and submits vouchers for reimbursement; HUD creates the grantee's account [1686](#cite:1686).

name: ezFedGrants (USDA)
what: [ezFedGrants](#term:ezfedgrants) is USDA's online system for applying for and managing USDA [grants](#term:grant) and agreements, described by the Office of the Chief Financial Officer as the department's system of record for [financial assistance](#term:financial-assistance) transactions [1929](#cite:1929). The page lists agency contacts for AMS, APHIS, FAS, [NIFA](#term:nifa), NRCS and OPPE [1929](#cite:1929).
applies_when: Applicants to and recipients of the USDA agencies that use the system [1929](#cite:1929). NIFA's own how-to-apply page directs applications to [Grants.gov](#term:grants-gov), not to ezFedGrants [1930](#cite:1930).
steps: Hold a [Login.gov](#term:login-gov) account linked to USDA eAuthentication [1929](#cite:1929).
Verify identity, online through Login.gov or in person at a USDA Service Center [1929](#cite:1929).
Request a user role in ezFedGrants [1929](#cite:1929).
time: No time is stated on the page read [1929](#cite:1929).
cost: No fee is stated on the page read [1929](#cite:1929).
renewal: None stated on the page read [1929](#cite:1929).

name: NIFA application route (Grants.gov, then ASAP for payment)
what: [NIFA](#term:nifa) publishes its funding opportunities and takes applications through [Grants.gov](#term:grants-gov), after the organisation has registered in [SAM.gov](#term:sam-gov) [1930](#cite:1930) [1976](#cite:1976). NIFA then screens each application and tells the applicant whether it is accepted, with a proposal number [1930](#cite:1930). Awardees draw funds through Treasury's [ASAP](#term:asap-payments) system [1931](#cite:1931). eRA lists NIFA among the agencies it supports [1913](#cite:1913).
applies_when: Organisations applying to NIFA competitive programmes [1930](#cite:1930).
steps: Register in SAM.gov and obtain the [UEI](#term:uei); renew annually [1930](#cite:1930).
Register in Grants.gov [1930](#cite:1930).
Prepare the application by the notice and by the version of the NIFA [Grants](#term:grant) Application Guide included in that opportunity's package [1976](#cite:1976).
Submit through Grants.gov; Grants.gov confirms receipt, and NIFA sends its acceptance or rejection after an administrative review [1930](#cite:1930).
Senior/key personnel complete the [Common Forms](#term:biosketch) in [SciENcv](#term:sciencv), as USDA's General Terms and Conditions effective December 31, 2025 require [1948](#cite:1948).
time: NIFA's page gives no time for registration [1930](#cite:1930).
cost: No fee is stated on the pages read; ASAP is provided at no charge to recipients [1931](#cite:1931).
renewal: SAM.gov registration must be renewed annually [1930](#cite:1930). USDA terms require an active SAM.gov registration until all final reports are submitted or final payment is received, whichever is later [1948](#cite:1948).

name: NEH eGMS Reach
what: [eGMS Reach](#term:egms-reach) is the online [grant](#term:grant) management system that [NEH](#term:neh) panelists and recipients use for all award management activities [1932](#cite:1932). Recipients use it for [prior approval](#term:prior-approval) and extension requests, reports and messages to NEH staff [1932](#cite:1932). Since January 20, 2023 it has been reached through [Login.gov](#term:login-gov) [1932](#cite:1932).
applies_when: The [project director](#term:principal-investigator) and the institutional grant administrator on an NEH award, each with a separate Login.gov account tied to the email address given to NEH [1932](#cite:1932).
steps: A person who already has a Login.gov account under the address given to NEH selects the Login.gov button [1932](#cite:1932).
A person whose Login.gov account uses another address adds the NEH address with 'Add Email' [1932](#cite:1932).
A new user creates a Login.gov account with the address given to NEH [1932](#cite:1932).
time: No time is stated on the page read [1932](#cite:1932).
cost: No fee is stated on the page read [1932](#cite:1932).
renewal: None stated on the page read [1932](#cite:1932).
common_problems: NEH warns that automatically forwarding eGMS Reach notifications to another address may cause them to be rejected, so that official messages are missed; shared accounts are not allowed [1932](#cite:1932).

name: ASAP.gov (Automated Standard Application for Payments) enrolment
what: [ASAP.gov](#term:asap-payments) is the Treasury system through which federal agencies transfer money to recipient organisations [1937](#cite:1937). The paying agency enrols the recipient, authorises its payments and manages its account [1937](#cite:1937). [NIFA](#term:nifa) awardees and DOJ recipients are paid through it [1931](#cite:1931) [1924](#cite:1924).
applies_when: Recipients of awards from agencies that pay through ASAP; enrolment begins only when the agency sends an invitation [1956](#cite:1956).
steps: The agency starts the enrolment, using the recipient's [UEI](#term:uei), [EIN](#term:ein), organisation type and point of contact [1956](#cite:1956).
The recipient's Point of Contact confirms the organisation's details and names the other officials [1956](#cite:1956).
The Authorizing Official confirms the information and names the people who will use ASAP [1956](#cite:1956).
The Financial Official enters the bank account information [1956](#cite:1956).
time: Treasury's page gives no time for the steps [1956](#cite:1956).
cost: Free for federal agencies and recipient organisations [1937](#cite:1937).
renewal: None stated on the pages read [1956](#cite:1956).

name: Federal Audit Clearinghouse (FAC) submission
what: The [Federal Audit Clearinghouse](#term:federal-audit-clearinghouse), run by GSA's Technology Transformation Services, is the repository of record to which an organisation submits its [single audit](#term:single-audit) [1881](#cite:1881) [1939](#cite:1939). A non-Federal entity that expends $1,000,000 or more in federal awards in a fiscal year must have a single or programme-specific audit; the FAC applies $750,000 to fiscal years that began before October 1, 2024 [1940](#cite:1940) [1938](#cite:1938). The FAC makes reporting packages public [1939](#cite:1939).
applies_when: Universities, non-profits and governments above the expenditure threshold; the subpart does not apply to for-profit organisations [1940](#cite:1940). An entity below the threshold is exempt from federal audit requirements for that year, though its records must remain available for review [1940](#cite:1940).
steps: Everyone who edits or certifies the submission creates a [Login.gov](#term:login-gov) account; credentials from the former Census Bureau clearinghouse do not work [1938](#cite:1938) [1881](#cite:1881).
Fill in the web forms and upload a PDF of the audit reporting package [1938](#cite:1938).
Submit the SF-SAC data collection form as a series of XLSX workbooks [1938](#cite:1938).
The certifying officials certify, and the auditee submits to the FAC [1939](#cite:1939) [1881](#cite:1881).
time: The submission is due within 30 calendar days after the auditee receives the auditor's report or nine months after the end of the audit period, whichever is earlier ([2 CFR 200](#term:uniform-guidance).512(a)) [1939](#cite:1939).
cost: No fee for submission is stated on the FAC pages read [1881](#cite:1881).
renewal: Yearly, for each fiscal year in which the threshold is met [1940](#cite:1940).

name: iEdison (invention reporting)
what: [iEdison](#term:iedison) is the interagency online system in which recipients of federal funding agreements report subject inventions to the funding agency and complete other reporting required under the Bayh-Dole Act [1951](#cite:1951). [NIH](#term:nih) built it in the 1990s and NIST has run it since around summer 2022 [1951](#cite:1951). The deadlines it serves are in the standard patent rights clause at 37 [CFR](#term:cfr) 401.14 [1952](#cite:1952).
applies_when: A recipient whose funded work produces an invention, where the funding agency takes reports through iEdison; NIST lists agencies as they join, most recently MDA (September 2026), DLA (August 2026) and USACE/ERDC (July 2026) [1951](#cite:1951).
steps: Register the organisation at iedison.nist.gov [1951](#cite:1951).
Each user holds an iEdison account and a [Login.gov](#term:login-gov) account under the same email address [1951](#cite:1951).
Disclose each subject invention to the agency within two months after the inventor discloses it in writing [1952](#cite:1952).
Elect whether to retain title within two years of disclosure, and file the initial patent application within one year after election [1952](#cite:1952).
Report on utilization when asked, no more often than annually [1952](#cite:1952).
time: No registration time is stated on the page read [1951](#cite:1951).
cost: No fee is stated on the page read [1951](#cite:1951).
renewal: None stated on the page read [1951](#cite:1951).

name: Federalwide Assurance (FWA) for the protection of human subjects
what: A [Federalwide Assurance](#term:human-subjects) is an institution's written promise to the federal government that it will follow the Common Rule, the shared federal regulation on research with human subjects [1981](#cite:1981) [1984](#cite:1984). It is filed with the Office for Human Research Protections (OHRP) in [HHS](#term:hhs) and is the only kind of assurance OHRP accepts [1988](#cite:1988). Other federal agencies accept an assurance on file with OHRP in place of one of their own [1981](#cite:1981).
applies_when: Every institution engaged in non-exempt human subjects research that is conducted or supported by HHS or another federal department or agency that follows the Common Rule needs one [1986](#cite:1986) [1984](#cite:1984). Research that is exempt under 45 [CFR](#term:cfr) 46.104 does not require an assurance [1981](#cite:1981). A collaborating investigator at an institution with no assurance can be covered by an Individual Investigator Agreement under another institution's FWA; OHRP says an institution where HHS-supported research routinely occurs obtains its own [1988](#cite:1988).
steps: Register the institutional review board the institution will rely on, or identify a registered one: an IRB must be registered before it can be designated under an assurance [1983](#cite:1983).
Go to OHRP's electronic submission system at ohrp.cit.nih.gov/efile/FwaStart.aspx and choose "I need a submission number" [1987](#cite:1987).
Enter an email address and password; the submission number arrives by email [1987](#cite:1987).
Return to the site, choose "I have a submission number", and complete and submit the FWA application [1987](#cite:1987).
The assurance is executed by an individual authorised to act for the institution, called the Signatory Official on OHRP's pages [1981](#cite:1981) [1984](#cite:1984).
Where the institution relies on an IRB it does not operate, the reliance and the division of responsibilities are documented [1981](#cite:1981).
cost: The OHRP pages read state no fee [1985](#cite:1985) [1988](#cite:1988).
renewal: An FWA is effective for 5 years and is renewed every 5 years, even if nothing has changed [1984](#cite:1984) [1988](#cite:1988). It is updated within 90 days after a change in the institution's legal name, its Human Protections Administrator or its Signatory Official [1984](#cite:1984). An approved electronic [renewal](#term:renewal) or update starts a new 5-year period [1988](#cite:1988). OHRP states that failure to renew or update while continuing covered research may constitute noncompliance [1984](#cite:1984).
common_problems: Federal support for covered research is given only if the institution has an assurance and, where certification is required, has certified that an IRB reviewed and approved the research; the research may not begin before that certification [1981](#cite:1981).

name: Institutional review board (IRB) registration with OHRP
what: An [institutional review board](#term:human-subjects) (IRB) reviews and approves research with human subjects; each IRB that reviews HHS-conducted or HHS-supported research, and each IRB designated under a Federalwide Assurance, must be registered with OHRP [1983](#cite:1983) [1989](#cite:1989). Registration records that the required information was provided; it is not a finding by OHRP that the IRB reviews research in line with the regulations [1989](#cite:1989).
applies_when: An institution that operates its own IRB registers it [1983](#cite:1983). An institution without its own IRB may rely on another registered IRB, with the reliance documented [1981](#cite:1981).
steps: Register electronically through http://ohrp.cit.nih.gov/efile; an institution unable to register electronically sends the information in writing [1983](#cite:1983).

Give the institution's name and address, a senior officer and a contact person, the IRB's name and chairperson, approximate numbers of active protocols and of those supported by [HHS](#term:hhs), and the staff time devoted to the IRB [1983](#cite:1983).
An initial registration covers both the institution or organisation (the IORG) and its IRB or IRBs [1989](#cite:1989).
Registration is effective when OHRP accepts it; the IRB can then be designated under an FWA [1983](#cite:1983).
cost: The OHRP pages read state no fee [1985](#cite:1985) [1989](#cite:1989).
renewal: Registration is effective for 3 years and is renewed every 3 years [1983](#cite:1983). A change of contact person or chairperson is reported within 90 days, and the disbanding of an IRB within 30 days after it permanently stops reviewing research [1983](#cite:1983). Any electronic update renews the registration of the organisation and its IRBs [1989](#cite:1989).

name: Education in the protection of human research participants
what: [NIH](#term:nih) requires investigators and all key personnel involved in the design or conduct of NIH-funded [human subjects](#term:human-subjects) research to complete education in the protection of human subjects, under NIH Guide notice NOT-OD-00-039 [1991](#cite:1991). NIH prescribes no particular course and no longer offers its own [1991](#cite:1991).
applies_when: The requirement applies to NIH-funded research with human subjects [1991](#cite:1991). Good Clinical Practice training is a separate NIH policy (NOT-OD-16-148) for clinical investigators and clinical trial staff involved in the design, conduct, oversight or management of NIH-funded clinical trials [2090](#cite:2090).
steps: Complete a course in human research protections; NIH points to the free Human Research Protection Training offered by OHRP [1991](#cite:1991) [2076](#cite:2076).
cost: OHRP's training materials are for public use and may be used and shared freely [2076](#cite:2076). NIH lists free Good Clinical Practice courses [2090](#cite:2090).
renewal: Good Clinical Practice training is refreshed every three years, and those trained keep documentation of it [2090](#cite:2090). The NIH human subjects education page states no [renewal](#term:renewal) interval [1991](#cite:1991).

pending_changes.text: NOT-OD-25-148 replaced OLAW's 2005 guidance on prompt reporting; it ties reporting to the scope of the institution's Assurance and adds examples of events not normally reported [2082](#cite:2082). The PHS Policy itself remains the 2015 edition [1999](#cite:1999).

name: Animal Welfare Assurance (OLAW) and the institutional animal care and use committee
what: An [Animal Welfare Assurance](#term:animal-welfare-assurance) is the document in which an institution describes its animal care and use programme and commits to the Public Health Service Policy on Humane Care and Use of Laboratory Animals [1994](#cite:1994) [1999](#cite:1999). No PHS-supported activity with live vertebrate animals may be conducted until the institution has an Assurance acceptable to the PHS, negotiated with the [NIH](#term:nih) Office of Laboratory Animal Welfare (OLAW) [1994](#cite:1994). OLAW's pages say the same Assurance covers NSF- and NASA-funded animal activities [1995](#cite:1995). There are three kinds: Domestic, for a United States institution doing the animal work on its own site; Foreign, for an institution outside the United States; and Interinstitutional, for an awardee with no animal programme of its own whose animal work is done at an assured institution [1995](#cite:1995) [1997](#cite:1997).
applies_when: The Assurance is needed when a PHS, [NSF](#term:nsf) or NASA award involves live vertebrate animals [1995](#cite:1995). A Domestic Assurance requires the institution to have its own animal facilities, an Institutional Official, an institutional animal care and use committee (IACUC) and a veterinarian with programme authority [1996](#cite:1996). An IACUC has at least five members, including a veterinarian, a practising scientist, a non-scientist and a person not affiliated with the institution [1999](#cite:1999). An Interinstitutional Assurance is for an institution that has no Assurance, no animal programme, no animal housing and no IACUC [1997](#cite:1997).
steps: An institution cannot apply unasked: OLAW does not accept or process [unsolicited](#term:unsolicited-request) applications [1994](#cite:1994).
The funding component notifies the institution and OLAW of a pending award, or of animal activities added to an award; OLAW then contacts the institution [1994](#cite:1994).
The institution completes the Assurance form for its type, signed by the Institutional Official; OLAW publishes sample documents [1994](#cite:1994) [1996](#cite:1996).
An OLAW reviewer asks for clarifications and the institution returns a revised version with changes marked [1994](#cite:1994).
The institution provides the final signed version; OLAW signs it and issues an approval letter [1994](#cite:1994).
time: The OLAW pages read give no time for the negotiation [1994](#cite:1994).
cost: The OLAW pages read state no fee [1994](#cite:1994).
renewal: OLAW's pages say Domestic and Foreign Assurances are approved for up to 4 years and Interinstitutional Assurances for the life of the [grant](#term:grant) or contract, up to 5 years [1996](#cite:1996) [1998](#cite:1998) [1997](#cite:1997). The PHS Policy page, as returned by the fetch, says approval is for no longer than five years [1999](#cite:1999). OLAW asks for a [renewal](#term:renewal) 4 months before expiry, and renews a Domestic Assurance only if the institution still conducts funded animal work on site [1994](#cite:1994) [1996](#cite:1996). An institution with a Domestic Assurance sends OLAW an annual report for the federal fiscal year, October 1 to September 30, due by December 1 [1996](#cite:1996) [2000](#cite:2000). A new Interinstitutional Assurance is needed if the institutions involved change [1997](#cite:1997).
common_problems: OLAW states that Assurance materials sent before OLAW has made contact are not processed [1994](#cite:1994). The IACUC must review the programme and inspect facilities at least every six months and review each ongoing activity completely at least every three years [1999](#cite:1999).

pending_changes.text: [NIH](#term:nih) released a Draft NIH Biosafety Policy for Research Involving Biohazards for public comment through October 19, 2026 (NOT-OD-26-112) [2001](#cite:2001).
Research activities identified as potential dangerous gain-of-function research remain paused until NIH sets implementation requirements (NOT-OD-25-112, NOT-OD-25-127) [2001](#cite:2001).

name: Institutional Biosafety Committee (IBC) registration under the NIH Guidelines
what: The NIH Guidelines for Research Involving Recombinant or Synthetic Nucleic Acid Molecules set safety practices and containment for that research; the edition in force is dated April 2024 [2001](#cite:2001). An institution covered by the Guidelines has an Institutional Biosafety Committee, which is registered and updated each year in NIH's IBC Registration Management System [2001](#cite:2001).
applies_when: The Guidelines cover basic and clinical research involving recombinant or synthetic nucleic acid molecules, including organisms and viruses that contain them [2001](#cite:2001).
steps: Register the committee and file annual updates in the IBC Registration Management System (IBC-RMS) [2001](#cite:2001).
Post the minutes of every committee meeting held on or after June 1, 2025 on a public-facing institutional website, under NOT-OD-25-082 [2001](#cite:2001).
renewal: The registration is updated annually [2001](#cite:2001).

name: Financial conflict of interest (FCOI) policy for PHS-funded research
what: An institution that applies for or receives Public Health Service research funding by [grant](#term:grant) or [cooperative agreement](#term:cooperative-agreement) must have a written, enforced policy on financial conflicts of interest and must post it on a public web site (42 [CFR](#term:cfr) 50.604(a)) [2002](#cite:2002). Investigators disclose their significant financial interests to the institution, which decides whether any of them is a conflict, manages it and reports it to the funding agency [2002](#cite:2002) [2003](#cite:2003). Phase I SBIR and STTR applications are outside the rule [2002](#cite:2002) [2003](#cite:2003).
applies_when: The rule applies to each institution applying for or receiving PHS research funding, [NIH](#term:nih) included, and through it to each investigator: the [project director](#term:principal-investigator) or principal investigator and any other person responsible for the design, conduct or reporting of the research [2002](#cite:2002) [2003](#cite:2003). A [subrecipient](#term:subrecipient) either follows its own compliant policy or the awardee's, as the written [subaward](#term:subaward) agreement states [2002](#cite:2002).
steps: The institution adopts a written, enforced policy and posts it on its public web site; NIH also requires the policy to be submitted through the [eRA Commons](#term:era-commons) Institution Profile (IPF) Module [2002](#cite:2002) [2003](#cite:2003).
Each investigator completes training before engaging in PHS-funded research and at least every four years [2002](#cite:2002).
Each investigator discloses significant financial interests no later than the time of application and updates the disclosure at least annually [2002](#cite:2002).

A significant financial interest exists when remuneration from a publicly traded entity in the preceding twelve months plus equity held exceeds $5,000, when remuneration from a non-publicly traded entity exceeds $5,000, or when the investigator holds any equity in a non-publicly traded entity [2002](#cite:2002).

The institution reports each identified conflict to the awarding component before spending award funds, and within sixty days for conflicts identified later; for NIH grants the report is filed in the eRA Commons FCOI Module [2002](#cite:2002) [2003](#cite:2003).
Information on conflicts held by senior/key personnel is made available on a public web site or by written response within five business days of a request [2002](#cite:2002).
By signing an application the [Authorized Organization Representative](#term:authorized-organization-representative) certifies the institution's compliance with the regulation [2003](#cite:2003).
cost: No fee is stated; NIH publishes an FCOI Policy Development Checklist, updated 06/29/2026, for institutions writing or revising a policy [2003](#cite:2003).
renewal: Training is repeated at least every four years and disclosures are updated at least annually [2002](#cite:2002). The policy is kept up to date [2002](#cite:2002).
common_problems: When a conflict is not identified or managed in time, the institution completes a retrospective review within 120 days of determining the noncompliance [2002](#cite:2002) [2003](#cite:2003).

name: NSF conflict of interest policy requirement
what: [NSF](#term:nsf) requires each recipient organisation that employs more than fifty persons to maintain a written and enforced conflict of interest policy ([PAPPG](#term:pappg) Chapter IX.A) [2004](#cite:2004). The [Authorized Organizational Representative](#term:authorized-organization-representative) certifies with each proposal that the policy is in place and that conflicts have been managed [257](#cite:257).
applies_when: The requirement applies to NSF recipient organisations with more than fifty employees [2004](#cite:2004). An interest is not a significant financial interest when it does not exceed $10,000 in value and does not represent more than a 5% ownership interest in any single entity [2004](#cite:2004).
steps: The organisation maintains a written and enforced policy [2004](#cite:2004).
Investigators give the organisation their financial disclosures at the time the proposal is submitted to NSF, and update them annually or when new reportable interests arise [2004](#cite:2004).
The organisation tells NSF's Office of the General Counsel if it finds it cannot satisfactorily manage a conflict [2004](#cite:2004).
Records of disclosures and of actions taken are kept at least three years beyond the end of the award [2004](#cite:2004).
renewal: Disclosures are updated annually during the award [2004](#cite:2004).

pending_changes.text: The revised 42 [CFR](#term:cfr) part 93 took effect January 1, 2025, and its requirements apply from January 1, 2026: institutions follow the revised part for allegations received on or after that date [2008](#cite:2008) [2006](#cite:2006). Policies and procedures required by the revised part are to be implemented by the due date of the annual report covering the 2025 reporting year [2006](#cite:2006); ORI's reporting window closes April 30 [2009](#cite:2009).

name: Research misconduct assurance filed with the Office of Research Integrity (ORI)
what: An institution is eligible for Public Health Service funding when it has an assurance on file with the [HHS](#term:hhs) Office of Research Integrity that it has written policies and procedures for handling allegations of research misconduct and follows them [2009](#cite:2009) [2007](#cite:2007). Research misconduct means fabrication, falsification or plagiarism in proposing, performing or reviewing research, or in reporting results [2006](#cite:2006). The governing rule, 42 CFR part 93, was revised by a [final rule](#term:final-rule) published September 17, 2024 [2008](#cite:2008).
applies_when: The assurance is required of institutions that receive PHS support for biomedical or behavioural research [2007](#cite:2007) [2008](#cite:2008).
steps: Adopt written policies and procedures for addressing allegations of research misconduct; ORI publishes a sample document titled for 2025 [2007](#cite:2007) [2011](#cite:2011).

Establish the assurance, either by signing the face page of a [grant](#term:grant) application ([SF 424](#term:sf-424) (R&R) or PHS 398) or by filing the Assurance Establishment Form, PHS-7091, on paper or online [2009](#cite:2009).
The Institutional Certifying Official assures compliance initially and then annually [2007](#cite:2007).
File the Annual Report on Possible Research Misconduct, PHS-6349, between January 1 and April 30 each year [2009](#cite:2009).

A small institution, described by ORI as typically 1 to 50 institutional members, may with ORI's approval file a Small Institution Statement in place of its own policies; it then reports every allegation to ORI, which works with it on the case [2010](#cite:2010) [2007](#cite:2007).
cost: The ORI pages read state no fee [2009](#cite:2009).
renewal: The assurance is kept active by the annual report, due between January 1 and April 30, and by keeping policies consistent with the regulation [2009](#cite:2009) [2007](#cite:2007). The ORI assurance page states no consequence for a missed report [2009](#cite:2009).
common_problems: Under the revised rule an inquiry is completed within 90 days of its start unless circumstances warrant longer, an investigation within 180 days, and records are kept for seven years [2006](#cite:2006).

name: Responsible conduct of research training (NIH RCR and NSF RECR)
what: [NIH](#term:nih)'s requirement for instruction in the responsible conduct of research attaches to research training, career development, research education and dissertation research [grants](#term:grant) [2013](#cite:2013). [NSF](#term:nsf)'s, which it calls responsible and ethical conduct of research (RECR), attaches to every proposal: the institution certifies a plan to train the undergraduate students, graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, faculty and other senior/key personnel supported by the project [2004](#cite:2004).
applies_when: At NIH, instruction is given at least once during each career stage and no less than once every four years [2013](#cite:2013). Video conferencing may be part of the instruction and, outside stated circumstances, is not the sole means [2013](#cite:2013). At NSF, training must include mentor training and mentorship, and the institution designates one or more persons to oversee compliance [2004](#cite:2004) [2005](#cite:2005).
steps: NIH: the institution's training or [career award](#term:nsf-career) application describes the instruction; subjects include conflict of interest, authorship, misconduct, data management and sharing, and the use of human participants and animals, with conflict of commitment, safe research environments and secure data use added in 2022 [2012](#cite:2012) [2013](#cite:2013).

NSF: the [Authorized Organizational Representative](#term:authorized-organization-representative) certifies with each proposal that the institution has a plan for RECR training and oversight [2004](#cite:2004) [257](#cite:257).
renewal: NIH instruction recurs at least every four years [2013](#cite:2013). NSF sets no interval in the chapter read [2004](#cite:2004).

pending_changes.text: [NIH](#term:nih) [rescinded](#term:rescission) its notice implementing the [research security programme](#term:research-security) certification and said updated guidance would follow [127](#cite:127). No later NIH date for that certification was found in this sweep [33](#cite:33).

name: Research security programme certification (covered institutions)
what: National Security Presidential Memorandum 33 requires research institutions that receive more than 50 million dollars a year in federal science and engineering support to certify to the funding agency that they have established and operate a research security programme [247](#cite:247) [2018](#cite:2018). An OSTP memorandum of July 9, 2024 set the content of such a programme and a timeline [2017](#cite:2017).
applies_when: A covered institution is an [institution of higher education](#term:institution-of-higher-education), a federally funded research and development centre or a non-profit research institution above the $50 million threshold, measured as a three-year average of federal research and development obligations [2017](#cite:2017). The threshold is stated in fiscal year 2022 constant dollars [2017](#cite:2017).
steps: Establish a programme with four elements: cybersecurity, foreign travel security, research security training and export control training [2017](#cite:2017).
Certify by a written or electronic attestation to a federal research agency [2017](#cite:2017).
time: Under the OSTP memorandum, agencies were to submit implementation plans within six months, their policies were to take effect no later than six months after that, and institutions have not more than 18 months from an agency's effective date to implement [2017](#cite:2017).
common_problems: [NSF](#term:nsf)'s guidelines page quotes the mandate and gives no NSF date or mechanism [2018](#cite:2018). NIH announced the requirement on September 11, 2025 for applications from January 25, 2026, rescinded that notice on September 29, 2025, and said an implementation date had not been finalised [2016](#cite:2016) [127](#cite:127). A law firm alert of March 2026 says there is no single government-wide deadline, because the 18 months run from each agency's own effective date [2022](#cite:2022). IARPA's page on its implementation of NSPM-33 says the research security programme certification deadline has yet to be finalised, and that it accepts proposals from covered institutions that are implementing a programme but are not yet certified; the page is undated [2111](#cite:2111). NSF's research security page, updated August 6, 2026, quotes the NSPM-33 mandate and gives no date or means of certification [247](#cite:247). NIH's notice of December 2, 2025 covers training only and does not mention the programme certification [33](#cite:33). USDA's General Terms and Conditions effective December 31, 2025 and its research security deviation of June 3, 2026 have no term on it [1948](#cite:1948) [2110](#cite:2110). NIST's research security questions and answers, last modified March 24, 2025, say that at present NIST does not require applicants to demonstrate the existence of a research security programme in order to apply for or receive funding [2115](#cite:2115).

name: NSF Foreign Financial Disclosure Report (FFDR)
what: Each [institution of higher education](#term:institution-of-higher-education) that receives [NSF](#term:nsf) funding reports each year its current financial support of $50,000 or more from a foreign source associated with a foreign country of concern, under section 10339B of the CHIPS and Science Act (42 U.S.C. 19040) [247](#cite:247). The report is filed in [Research.gov](#term:research-gov) [247](#cite:247) [2014](#cite:2014).
applies_when: The report applies to direct recipients of NSF awards that are institutions of higher education [2014](#cite:2014). The countries of concern named are China, North Korea, Russia and Iran, with others the Secretary of State may designate [2014](#cite:2014).
steps: File the report in Research.gov for the period July 1 through June 30; for the period ending June 30, 2025 the portal opened September 1, 2025 and the report was due October 31, 2025 [2014](#cite:2014).
renewal: The report is annual [247](#cite:247). The dates for the period ending June 30, 2026 were not found in this sweep [2014](#cite:2014).

pending_changes.text: A new reporting portal went live January 2, 2026; the announcement said existing guidance and deadlines initially remained unchanged [2026](#cite:2026).

A law firm alert reports that the Departments of Education and State announced an interagency agreement under which the State Department assists with section 117 reporting and enforcement, and that [Executive Order](#term:executive-order) 14282 of April 23, 2025 directed enforcement of the section [2027](#cite:2027). The agencies' own documents were not read in this sweep [2027](#cite:2027).

Executive Order 14282, "Transparency Regarding Foreign Influence at American Universities", was signed April 23, 2025 and published April 28, 2025 at 90 FR 17541 [2106](#cite:2106). It directs the Secretary of Education, with the Attorney General, to require disclosure of the sources and purposes of foreign funding, to make the information public and to use audits and investigations; it directs agencies to treat certification of compliance with section 117 as material under the False Claims Act and says federal [grant](#term:grant) funds are not to be provided in cases of noncompliance [2106](#cite:2106). The order as read names no deadline [2106](#cite:2106).

The Department of Education's press release of February 23, 2026 says Education and State are establishing a partnership under which State will support Education in managing the section 117 foreign funding reporting portal, review and assess compliance with the law, share data with the public and federal stakeholders, and identify potential threats [1397](#cite:1397). The release gives no date on which State takes up the work and no change to the reporting deadlines, and does not say whether Education keeps an enforcement role [1397](#cite:1397).

The Department of Education's announcements of June 18 and July 6, 2026 kept the semiannual date and the $250,000 threshold: the next deadline was Friday, July 31, 2026, filed in the portal at ForeignFundingHigherEd.gov [2113](#cite:2113) [2112](#cite:2112). Since June 18, 2026 an institution can amend all its earlier reports in the portal, including those made before January 2, 2026, and questions go to foreignsourcereporting@ed.gov [2113](#cite:2113). An update of July 24, 2026 says the Department delayed until August 12, 2026 its planned publication of the names of all foreign sources from prior reporting cycles [2112](#cite:2112). On June 29, 2026 the Department sent [OMB](#term:omb) a [renewal](#term:renewal) of substantially the same information collection, control number 1845-0172, on the new portal [2114](#cite:2114). Neither announcement mentions the Department of State [2113](#cite:2113) [2112](#cite:2112).

name: Foreign gift and contract reporting (section 117 of the Higher Education Act)
what: An [institution of higher education](#term:institution-of-higher-education) that receives [federal financial assistance](#term:financial-assistance) reports to the Secretary of Education any gift from, or contract with, a foreign source worth $250,000 or more, alone or combined with others from the same source in a calendar year (20 U.S.C. 1011f) [2024](#cite:2024) [2025](#cite:2025). The Attorney General enforces the section by civil action [2024](#cite:2024).
applies_when: The statute covers institutions that award a bachelor's or higher degree, are accredited and receive federal financial assistance [2024](#cite:2024). The reporting duty rests on institutions that meet that definition [2024](#cite:2024).
steps: File a disclosure report on January 31 or July 31, whichever is sooner after the gift or contract [2024](#cite:2024).

File through the Section 117 Foreign Gifts and Contracts Reporting Portal at ForeignFundingHigherEd.gov, which went live January 2, 2026 and replaced the portal that closed December 16, 2025 [2026](#cite:2026).
The institution's Primary Destination Point Administrator authorises its users and attests to submissions [2026](#cite:2026).
Restricted or conditional gifts are disclosed separately with their conditions [2024](#cite:2024).
renewal: Reports are semiannual [2025](#cite:2025).
common_problems: The Attorney General may bring a civil action to compel compliance, and an institution that knowingly or willfully fails to comply pays the full costs of obtaining compliance [2024](#cite:2024).

pending_changes.text: GSA proposed to revise the [Financial Assistance](#term:financial-assistance) General Representations and Certifications to align with [Executive Order](#term:executive-order) 14173 and a Department of Justice guidance memorandum of July 29, 2025; comments closed March 30, 2026 and the notice states no effective date (91 FR 3726) [1866](#cite:1866). Secondary sources describe three added certifications, on antidiscrimination law and programmes labelled DEI, on immigration, and on funding or facilitating violence or terrorism [1970](#cite:1970) [2083](#cite:2083). No final action was found in this sweep [1866](#cite:1866).

Checked on 2026-10-04: the [Federal Register](#term:federal-register) index holds no later GSA document on the collection than the notice of January 28, 2026, and [OMB](#term:omb)'s record for control number 3090-0290 shows no request received in 2025 or 2026 [2099](#cite:2099) [2100](#cite:2100). A public comment filed in GSA's docket quotes four proposed certifications, on unlawful discrimination on the basis of race or color, on immigration, on funding or facilitating violence or terrorism, and on freedom of speech and religious liberty; GSA's own posting of the wording was not read [2109](#cite:2109).

name: Financial assistance certifications and representations in SAM.gov (successor to the SF-424B)
what: The governmentwide assurances that applicants once signed on Standard Form 424B, Assurances for Non-Construction Programs, are now made in [SAM.gov](#term:sam-gov) when an organisation registers or renews its registration [2035](#cite:2035). The General Services Administration began building the financial assistance certifications into SAM registration on February 2, 2019, and by February 2, 2020 every registrant had completed them [2035](#cite:2035). The [Uniform Guidance](#term:uniform-guidance) authorises agencies to require these certifications yearly (2 CFR 200.209) [2034](#cite:2034).
applies_when: Every organisation that registers in SAM.gov for financial assistance makes the certifications [2035](#cite:2035). [NSF](#term:nsf)'s policy guide says the governmentwide certifications, including debarment and suspension, lobbying and nondiscrimination, are provided annually in SAM [257](#cite:257). Where an agency excepts an applicant from SAM registration, it collects the assurance form itself [2034](#cite:2034).
steps: Complete the Financial Assistance General Certifications and Representations while registering or renewing in SAM.gov [2035](#cite:2035) [1866](#cite:1866).

Make any further certifications the agency adds in its own application or award terms; NSF lists nine of its own, and the Arts Endowment says an applicant certifies by signing and submitting its application on [Grants.gov](#term:grants-gov) [257](#cite:257) [656](#cite:656).
time: GSA's 2026 notice estimates 2.75 hours per response for the SAM registration requirements as a whole [1866](#cite:1866).
renewal: The certifications are renewed with the yearly SAM.gov registration [2034](#cite:2034) [257](#cite:257).

name: HHS Assurance of Compliance (Form HHS-690)
what: Form HHS-690 is the civil rights assurance that an organisation receiving [HHS](#term:hhs) [financial assistance](#term:financial-assistance) files with the HHS Office for Civil Rights [2036](#cite:2036) [528](#cite:528). In it the applicant agrees to comply with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, the Age Discrimination Act of 1975, section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act and federal conscience provisions [2036](#cite:2036).
applies_when: Domestic recipients, [subrecipients](#term:subrecipient) and contractors under HHS awards file it [528](#cite:528). At [NIH](#term:nih) the form must be on file with the HHS Office for Civil Rights before an award is made to a domestic organisation, and the [Authorized Organization Representative](#term:authorized-organization-representative)'s signature on an application certifies that it is [2088](#cite:2088).
steps: A person authorised to commit the applicant signs the form [2036](#cite:2036).
File it once with the Office for Civil Rights, by mail or through its online portal; it is not needed with each application [528](#cite:528) [2036](#cite:2036).
renewal: The form is filed once; the assurance binds the applicant's successors and transferees and is a material condition of continued federal financial assistance [528](#cite:528) [2036](#cite:2036).
common_problems: The copy of the form read carries an [OMB](#term:omb) expiry date of 04/30/2026; whether a renewed form has replaced it was not established [2036](#cite:2036). Separately, the HHS [Grants](#term:grant) Policy Statement in force since October 1, 2025 says that by accepting an award a recipient certifies compliance with Title IX, including requirements in [Executive Order](#term:executive-order) 14168, and with Title VI [528](#cite:528). The change ledger records a court order on new HHS grant conditions under the id ch-sb-hhs-hud-new-grant-conditions-vacated; that order was not read in this sweep [528](#cite:528).

name: Lobbying certification and disclosure (31 U.S.C. 1352)
what: A person who requests or receives a federal [grant](#term:grant) or [cooperative agreement](#term:cooperative-agreement) of more than $100,000 files a certification, and a disclosure form if one is required [2039](#cite:2039). [HHS](#term:hhs) describes the certification as a statement that the applicant has not made [unallowable](#term:allowable-cost) lobbying payments and will report non-federal funds used for lobbying [528](#cite:528). The rule comes from section 319 of Public Law 101-121 (31 U.S.C. 1352) and each agency codifies it; HHS's version is 45 [CFR](#term:cfr) part 93 [2039](#cite:2039).
applies_when: The threshold is an award exceeding $100,000 for grants, cooperative agreements and contracts, and $150,000 for loans and loan guarantees [2039](#cite:2039). HHS applies the certification to applicants with total proposed costs of more than $100,000 [528](#cite:528).
steps: Certify when asking for the award and again on receiving it unless already filed; at [NSF](#term:nsf) the governmentwide certification is made in [SAM.gov](#term:sam-gov) [2039](#cite:2039) [257](#cite:257).

File the disclosure form, Standard Form LLL (Disclosure of Lobbying Activities), where it applies: the Office of Justice Programs requires it if the applicant has paid or will pay anyone to lobby and the award exceeds $100,000, and an [NEH](#term:neh) notice lists it as conditionally required [619](#cite:619) [648](#cite:648).
Collect certifications from [subrecipients](#term:subrecipient) above $100,000 and pass disclosure forms up, tier by tier, to the agency [2039](#cite:2039).
renewal: A disclosure is updated at the end of any calendar quarter in which an event materially affects its accuracy, such as a cumulative increase of $25,000 or more in lobbying payments [2039](#cite:2039).

name: Drug-free workplace requirements
what: Under the Drug-Free Workplace Act (41 U.S.C. 8101-8106) and 2 [CFR](#term:cfr) part 182, a [grant](#term:grant) recipient other than an individual publishes a drug-free workplace statement and runs an ongoing drug-free awareness programme [2037](#cite:2037).
applies_when: The requirement applies to recipients of [federal financial assistance](#term:financial-assistance); an individual recipient has a narrower duty not to engage in unlawful drug activity related to the award [2037](#cite:2037).
steps: Publish the statement, establish the awareness programme and identify all known workplaces under each award [2037](#cite:2037).

Tell the agency within ten calendar days of learning that an employee working on the award was convicted of a drug violation, and take personnel action or require rehabilitation within 30 calendar days [2037](#cite:2037).
common_problems: Sanctions for a violation include suspension of payments, suspension or [termination](#term:termination) of the award, and suspension or debarment for up to five years [2037](#cite:2037).

name: Debarment and suspension disclosures and checks
what: An applicant tells the agency whether it or any of its principals is excluded from federal awards, has been convicted of or found civilly liable for listed offences within three years, is presently indicted or charged, or has had a public transaction [terminated](#term:termination) for cause or default within three years (2 [CFR](#term:cfr) 180.335) [2038](#cite:2038). A recipient also checks the parties it pays under the award [2038](#cite:2038).
applies_when: The disclosure covers the organisation and its principals; [HHS](#term:hhs) names [principal investigators](#term:principal-investigator) and other key personnel among them [528](#cite:528). Agencies follow the governmentwide guidance in 2 CFR part 180 when they review an applicant [2023](#cite:2023).
steps: Disclose the four matters before entering into the award [2038](#cite:2038) [528](#cite:528).

Before a covered transaction with a lower-tier party, verify that the party is not excluded by checking [SAM.gov](#term:sam-gov) Exclusions, collecting a certification, or adding a clause or condition to the transaction [2038](#cite:2038).

name: Recognition of exemption under section 501(c)(3) (Form 1023 or Form 1023-EZ)
what: An organisation becomes a non-profit under state law and becomes tax-exempt under federal law; the two are separate steps [2047](#cite:2047). To be recognised as exempt under [section 501(c)(3)](#term:section-501c3) of the Internal Revenue Code an organisation applies to the IRS on [Form 1023](#term:form-1023) or, if it is small enough, on the shorter Form 1023-EZ [2046](#cite:2046) [2049](#cite:2049). Federal notices that admit "nonprofits having a 501(c)(3) status with the IRS" rest on this recognition [2064](#cite:2064).
applies_when: Form 1023-EZ is open only to an organisation that answers "No" to every question on its eligibility worksheet [2050](#cite:2050). The first three questions ask whether annual gross receipts are projected to exceed $50,000 in any of the next 3 years, whether they exceeded $50,000 in any of the past 3 years, and whether total assets have a fair market value above $250,000 [2050](#cite:2050). Churches, schools, hospitals, foreign organisations, successors to for-profit entities, [supporting organisations](#term:supporting-organization), private [operating foundations](#term:operating-foundation) and limited liability companies cannot use the short form [2050](#cite:2050). Every other applicant uses Form 1023 [2049](#cite:2049).
steps: Form the organisation under state law as a trust, a corporation or an association, and gather its organising documents [2047](#cite:2047).
Determine the state's registration requirements [2047](#cite:2047).

Obtain an [employer identification number (EIN)](#term:ein) for the new organisation; the online application is free, an approved EIN is issued immediately, and a corporation is formed with the state before applying [2047](#cite:2047) [2089](#cite:2089).
For the short form, read the instructions and complete the eligibility worksheet [2049](#cite:2049).

Register for an account on Pay.gov, search for "1023" or "1023-EZ", complete the form and pay the user fee there; Form 1023 has had to be filed electronically since January 31, 2020 [2048](#cite:2048) [2046](#cite:2046) [2051](#cite:2051).

The IRS issues a [determination letter](#term:determination-letter); determination letters can be looked up in the [Tax Exempt Organization Search](#term:tax-exempt-organization-search) [2059](#cite:2059) [2053](#cite:2053).
time: The IRS says it issues 80% of Form 1023-EZ determinations within 22 days and 80% of Form 1023 determinations within 191 days; the page was last updated June 28, 2026 [2053](#cite:2053). Form 1023-EZ applications cannot be expedited [2053](#cite:2053).
cost: The user fee is $600 for Form 1023 and $275 for Form 1023-EZ, paid through Pay.gov when the application is filed [2051](#cite:2051). Fees are set each year by revenue procedure, for 2026 Revenue Procedure 2026-5 [2052](#cite:2052).
renewal: Recognition is lost automatically if the organisation fails to file its annual return or notice for three consecutive years [2057](#cite:2057). If the application is filed within 27 months after the end of the month in which the organisation was formed and is approved, exemption runs from the date of formation [2050](#cite:2050).
common_problems: An approved application and its supporting documents are open to public inspection [2050](#cite:2050). A funder or donor checks an organisation's standing in the Tax Exempt Organization Search, and the IRS warns of delays in that tool's data [2059](#cite:2059).

name: Annual Form 990-series return or notice
what: A tax-exempt organisation files a return or an electronic notice with the IRS every year; which form depends on its size and on whether it is a [private foundation](#term:private-foundation) [2055](#cite:2055). An organisation that does not file for three consecutive years automatically loses its tax-exempt status [2057](#cite:2057).
applies_when: Gross receipts normally $50,000 or less: Form 990-N, the e-Postcard [2055]. Gross receipts under $200,000 and total assets under $500,000: Form 990-EZ or Form 990 [2055]. Gross receipts of $200,000 or more, or total assets of $500,000 or more: [Form 990](#term:form-990) [2055](#cite:2055). A private foundation files [Form 990-PF](#term:form-990-pf) whatever its size [2055](#cite:2055). Churches and conventions or associations of churches are excepted from filing [2056](#cite:2056).
steps: File the form that matches the organisation's gross receipts and assets each year; an organisation eligible for the e-Postcard may choose to file a full return [2055](#cite:2055).
renewal: The filing is annual [2055](#cite:2055). After three consecutive missed years revocation takes effect on the original due date of the third return or notice [2057](#cite:2057). The organisation is then removed from the IRS list of organisations eligible for deductible contributions, appears on the [Automatic Revocation List](#term:automatic-revocation), and is no longer eligible to receive tax-deductible contributions [2057](#cite:2057).
common_problems: A revoked organisation must apply again, with the user fee, to be reinstated [2057](#cite:2057) [2058](#cite:2058). Revenue Procedure 2014-11 gives four routes [2058](#cite:2058). An organisation that was eligible to file Form 990-EZ or 990-N in the three years and has not been revoked before may use streamlined retroactive reinstatement if it applies within 15 months [2058](#cite:2058). Others may seek retroactive reinstatement with a statement of reasonable cause, for at least one year if within 15 months and for all three years if later [2058](#cite:2058). Otherwise reinstatement runs only from the post-mark date of the new application [2058](#cite:2058).

name: State charitable solicitation registration
what: The IRS states that many states have laws regulating the [solicitation](#term:program-solicitation) of funds for charitable purposes, and that these generally require an organisation to register with a state agency before soliciting that state's residents [2062](#cite:2062). State statutes exempt certain categories of organisation and may also require periodic financial reports [2062](#cite:2062).
applies_when: The requirement depends on each state in which the organisation asks for contributions [2062](#cite:2062).
steps: Find the charity regulator for each state concerned in the directory kept by the National Association of State Charity Officials, to which the IRS points [2062](#cite:2062) [2063](#cite:2063).

pending_changes.text: Subpart C of 2 [CFR](#term:cfr) part 910 took effect August 17, 2026; it is the amendment the eCFR shows as the latest to title 2 when read on 2026-10-04 [2096](#cite:2096) [2102](#cite:2102) [2095](#cite:2095).

name: DOE conflict of interest and conflict of commitment policy (2 CFR part 910, subpart C)
what: The Department of Energy's [final rule](#term:final-rule) of July 16, 2026 (91 FR 43511) adds conflict of interest and conflict of commitment requirements to its [financial assistance](#term:financial-assistance) regulations as subpart C of 2 CFR part 910 [2096](#cite:2096). A non-Federal entity that applies for or holds a DOE financial assistance award must maintain a written policy on both kinds of conflict [2096](#cite:2096). On its effective date, August 17, 2026, the subpart superseded DOE's interim conflict of interest policy, FAL No. 2022-02 [2096](#cite:2096).
applies_when: Any non-Federal entity that is an applicant to or recipient of a DOE financial assistance award on or after August 17, 2026 [2096](#cite:2096). The rule as read states no minimum award amount and gives no waiver to an entity that already follows the Public Health Service or [NSF](#term:nsf) policy; programmes of the DOE Office of Indian Energy are excepted [2096](#cite:2096). A [subrecipient](#term:subrecipient) either certifies that its own policy complies or comes under the recipient's policy [2096](#cite:2096).
steps: The organisation adopts a written conflict of interest and conflict of commitment policy (910.210(a) as returned) [2096](#cite:2096).

Each covered individual, a person who contributes in a substantive, meaningful way to the development or execution of the scope of work of a project, discloses significant financial interests; the rule sets the threshold at remuneration or equity exceeding $5,000 in the 12 months before disclosure, or any equity interest in a non-publicly traded entity [2096](#cite:2096) [2096](#cite:2096).
Covered individuals complete training before engaging in a DOE-funded project [2096](#cite:2096).

The organisation reports to DOE any conflict that cannot be eliminated or managed, and any conflict involving a foreign government, its instrumentalities or a foreign-controlled entity [2096](#cite:2096).
Disclosures use the uniform Disclosure Certification Statement in Appendix A to the subpart [2096](#cite:2096).
renewal: Covered individuals update their disclosures annually and as soon as practicable, but not later than 15 days, after a new conflict arises; refresher training is required at least every two years; organisational conflicts are reported within fifteen days of learning of the conflict [2096](#cite:2096).
common_problems: DOE declined commenters' request for a one-year lead time and made the rule effective 30 days after publication [2096](#cite:2096). The two-year training cycle differs from the four-year cycle commenters asked DOE to match [2096](#cite:2096).

name: American Heart Association Professional Membership
what: An applicant for an AHA research award must be an AHA Professional Member when the proposal is submitted [2188](#cite:2188).
applies_when: Stated for the [Career Development Award](#term:k-award); the Association-wide rule was not read [2188](#cite:2188).

name: HHMI Application and Review Channel (ARC)
what: HHMI's own system for applications to its competitions, at arc.hhmi.org [2163](#cite:2163) [2162](#cite:2162).
applies_when: Applicants to the Freeman Hrabowski Scholars and Hanna H. Gray Fellows competitions [2162](#cite:2162) [2163](#cite:2163).

name: W. M. Keck Foundation designated institutional liaison
what: Each applicant institution has a designated liaison, and only that person may submit to the Keck Research Program [2133](#cite:2133). A researcher finds the liaison through the central development office [2134](#cite:2134).
applies_when: Every application to the Keck Research Program [2133](#cite:2133).

name: Applicant account in a foundation's Fluxx portal
what: Kellogg, Kresge, Mellon and Packard each run their own [grants](#term:grant) portal on the Fluxx system; an applicant registers separately with each foundation before it can submit [2269](#cite:2269) [2273](#cite:2273) [2339](#cite:2339) [2367](#cite:2367). Mellon's 2026 [open call](#term:open-call) required registration by December 1, 2025 for an application deadline of February 17, 2026 [2339](#cite:2339).

name: Registration in the RWJF application system (my.rwjf.org)
what: Applicants to a Robert Wood Johnson Foundation call register at my.rwjf.org and submit through the foundation's online system [2336](#cite:2336).

name: The Duke Endowment online portal (Blackbaud)
what: The Duke Endowment takes [pre-applications](#term:pre-application) in an online portal that opens six weeks before each deadline, and full applications in its Blackbaud grantee portal [2310](#cite:2310).

name: Robert W. Woodruff Foundation application portal (Blackbaud YourCause)
what: The Woodruff Foundation takes each application as a single PDF uploaded to Blackbaud's YourCause portal [2313](#cite:2313).

name: Knight Foundation open-call portal (Submittable)
what: The 2026 Knight Cities Challenge took applications at kf.submittable.com [2355](#cite:2355).
